summary:
A Biomedical Bracelet for Space Missions (BBSM) was developed. It is a wearable device designed to monitor physiological and environmental conditions and assist astronauts during their time in microgravity and the critical phase of re-entry into Earth's atmosphere.

A chatbot was also created as a preventive medical and psychological health support system, which will be integrated into the bracelet in the future.

This project is important because it allows the monitoring of physiological changes experienced by astronauts during space missions, especially when exposed to significant environmental changes. It also aims to provide support both during missions and after returning to Earth, helping astronauts receive appropriate medical care and achieve a faster recovery.
details:
BBSM (Biomedical Bracelet for Space Missions) is a biomedical bracelet with an artificial intelligence chatbot.

What does it do and how does it work?

BBSM continuously monitors radiation dose rate (µSv/h), oxygen saturation (SpO₂), heart rate (BPM), physical activity and movement, body temperature, and sleep quality (hours slept, awakenings, and sleep efficiency). If it detects an anomaly or a sudden change in any metric, the chatbot asks the astronaut a quick question about it to understand what is happening. If the change persists, it suggests activities or exercises. To provide evidence-based answers, the system uses scientific information and NASA resources.

What are its benefits?

Detects health changes early, without relying solely on the astronaut to notice them.

Lets astronauts quickly report symptoms and record physical changes right from the wrist.

Provides reliable, evidence-based health information.

Monitors radiation, a risk specific to space, alongside vital signs.

Offers exercise recommendations to counter the effects of microgravity.

What is the expected impact?

We want astronauts to have more autonomy to take care of their health on long, distant missions, where medical help from Earth is not immediate. Early detection of problems such as bone loss, cardiovascular changes, radiation exposure, or poor rest reduces risks and supports mission success.

This device can also continue to be used on Earth to keep tracking and measuring changes in the astronaut’s body.

Tools, hardware, and software used

Hardware: ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 microcontroller, MAX30102 sensor (pulse and oxygen), AD8232 module, ICM-20948 inertial sensor (movement), DFRobot Gravity Geiger counter (radiation), temperature sensor, microphone and speaker to interact with the chatbot, LiPo battery with TP4056 charging module (USB-C), and AMS1117-3.3 voltage regulator. We designed the circuit in EasyEDA.

Software: An AI chatbot fed with scientific information and NASA resources. We used JavaScript with Node.js for the code.

How is it creative?

It combines vital sign monitoring, radiation measurement, and an AI chatbot that talks with the astronaut in a single bracelet. Instead of just displaying numbers, the bracelet detects an anomaly, asks a contextual question, and recommends exercises, like a personal medical assistant on the wrist.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered the real risks of long missions (radiation, microgravity, isolation, and sleep) and wanted the device to be portable and comfortable, in the form of a bracelet. We also aimed for the answers to be based on scientific and NASA evidence, and for the interaction to be quick, with short questions so as not to distract the astronaut.

1. Current Development Status

The BBSM project is currently in development. We have developed an AI chatbot designed to provide preventive medical and psychological support using scientific information and NASA resources. The biomedical bracelet is being developed to monitor astronauts' physiological and environmental conditions. Future stages will focus on integrating the chatbot with the bracelet to create a more complete health monitoring system.

2. Multilingual Support

The chatbot supports three languages: English, Spanish, and German, allowing astronauts to interact with the system in their preferred language. This feature aims to improve communication and make health information more accessible during space missions.

3. Future Improvements

Future improvements include connecting the biomedical bracelet to the chatbot, developing a health monitoring dashboard, and storing physiological data to track changes over time. These improvements aim to support early detection of potential health risks and assist astronauts during missions and recovery on Earth.

BBSM – AI Virtual Health Assistant

The BBSM Virtual Assistant is an AI-powered chatbot designed to provide preventive medical and psychological support to astronauts during space missions. It uses scientific information and NASA resources to answer health-related questions, provide general recommendations, and support astronaut well-being. The assistant supports English, Spanish, and German, and is planned to be integrated into the biomedical bracelet in the future.

BBSM – Biomedical Bracelet for Space Missions

Hardware Architecture Description (BBME-v1.0)

The hardware design of the bracelet is structured into four main modular subsystems integrated around a high-performance, low-power core:

1. Processing and User Interface

Central Microcontroller (U1): ESP32-S3 SuperMini, featuring a dual-core Xtensa LX7 processor (up to 240 MHz), Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth LE capabilities, providing sufficient GPIOs and native communication buses (I2C, I2S, SPI) to manage all sensors concurrently.

Display (U2): 0.96-inch OLED screen (SSD1306 controller) for real-time visual telemetry and system status readout.

User Controls (KEY1, KEY2): Tactile micro-switches for menu navigation and Push-to-Talk (PTT) communication functionality.

2. Biomedical and Environmental Sensors

Cardiovascular Monitoring (PPG & ECG):

MAX30102 (U4): Optical pulse oximetry and heart rate sensor via I2C.

AD8232 (U5): Single-lead heart rate monitor for surface ECG electrical activity, working alongside the PPG to estimate blood pressure (Pulse Transit Time).

Neuromuscular & Bone Density Assessment:

MyoWare 2.0 (P1): Surface electromyography (sEMG) sensor to track muscle tone and fatigue on the forearm.

AD5940: High-precision bioelectrical impedance spectroscopy (BIA) chip used to estimate bone mineral density changes and body fluid composition via skin-contact electrodes.

Vestibular & Motion Stability:

ICM-20948 (U6): 9-axis Inertial Measurement Unit (accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer) via I2C to detect spatial disorientation and gait instability.

Environmental Radiation:

DFRobot SEN0463 (U7): Geiger-Müller counter module connected via digital interrupt to monitor ionizing radiation dose rates in real time.

3. Digital Audio Subsystem (I2S Bus)

Microphone (MIC1): INMP441 omnidirectional MEMS digital microphone utilizing an I2S interface for high-clarity voice input.

Audio Output (U3, SPK1): MAX98357A Class D amplifier with an integrated DAC, coupled with a miniature

8Ω

8Ω speaker to render voice feedback and audio alerts without analog noise interference.

4. Power Management, Protection, and Actuators

Power Source (U8, U11): 3.7V rechargeable LiPo flat battery (~800 mAh) paired with a TP4056 charging module featuring USB-C connectivity and over-discharge protection.

Power Gating / Energy Optimization (Q2, Q3): IRLML6402 P-channel MOSFETs designed to completely cut power to high-consumption sensors (such as the Geiger counter and audio amplifier) during idle or deep-sleep states.

Haptic Feedback & Safety (U10, Q1): Coin-type mini vibration motor driven safely via a 2N2222 NPN transistor (Q1), a base resistor (R1), and a 1N4148 flyback protection diode (D1).
